description: The Almighty as One, Creator, Law-Giver and Judge; the Shekhinah; and Jewish beliefs about the Messiah.
content_html:
The Nature of the Almighty

The Edexcel spec uses the title ‘the Almighty’ as the formal name for God in Judaism. Jewish belief is centred on the absolute oneness of the Almighty — monotheism is foundational. The Almighty is One: not one of many gods, not a God with parts or persons, but the absolutely singular source and sustainer of all existence. This is stated in the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4): “Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one.”

Genesis 2 is the named source for several of the Almighty’s key characteristics:

Creator: The Almighty is the Creator of all existence, bringing the universe into being from nothing (creation ex nihilo). Genesis 2 describes the Almighty forming man from the dust of the ground and breathing life into him — humanity has a special, intimate relationship with the Creator. Jews today see creation as a gift requiring responsible stewardship.

Law-Giver: The Almighty is the source of all moral and religious law. The Torah (especially the Ten Commandments in Exodus 20) represents the Almighty’s revealed law. Living according to the Almighty’s law is not merely a religious duty but the means by which Jewish individuals and communities reflect the divine will in everyday life.

Judge: The Almighty holds all humanity accountable for their actions. Jewish theology teaches that the Almighty sees all deeds, knows all intentions, and will judge righteously. This belief in divine justice motivates ethical living — if the Almighty judges, then moral behaviour ultimately matters.

Key Fact

The four Edexcel-named characteristics of the Almighty: One (absolute monotheism — Shema, Deuteronomy 6:4), Creator (Genesis 2), Law-Giver (Torah, Exodus 20), Judge (holds all humanity accountable). These characteristics are tested in 3-mark and 4-mark questions.

The Shekhinah

Shekhinah means ‘divine dwelling’ — the presence of the Almighty among the Jewish people. The named anchor text is 2 Chronicles 7:1–3, which describes the Shekhinah descending as a cloud and filling the Temple when Solomon dedicated it: “When Solomon had finished praying, fire came down from heaven and consumed the burnt offering… and the glory of the Lord filled the temple.” The priests could not enter because of the overwhelming divine presence.

The Shekhinah is both comforting and awesome. Jewish theology developed the concept to express how the transcendent, infinite Almighty can be encountered in human experience — in the Temple, in the synagogue, in the home, and wherever Jews gather to pray. For many Jews, the Shekhinah is also associated with the feminine aspect of the divine.

Orthodox Judaism maintains that the Shekhinah was uniquely present in the Temple and that its absence today (since the Temple’s destruction in 70 CE) is a mark of divine distance pending the Messianic age and the rebuilding of the Temple. The Shekhinah will return fully when the Messiah comes. Reform Judaism tends to understand the Shekhinah as God’s presence available in every genuine moment of prayer, community and ethical action — not waiting for a physical Temple. This makes the concept more immediately accessible but less tied to specific historical events.

The Messiah and the Messianic Age

Messiah comes from the Hebrew mashiach (‘anointed one’). In Judaism the Messiah is a future human king — not divine — from the lineage of King David who will redeem the Jewish people and bring a universal age of peace. The named anchor text is Jeremiah 23:5–8, which describes the Almighty promising to raise a righteous Branch from David’s line who will reign wisely and bring justice: “The days are coming… when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, a King who will reign wisely and do what is just and right in the land.”

The messianic age will involve: the ingathering of exiled Jews to Israel; the rebuilding of the Temple in Jerusalem; universal recognition of the Almighty; the end of war and injustice. Jews believe the Messianic age has not yet arrived — the world still contains war, injustice and suffering.

Key Fact

Orthodox Jews believe in a personal Messiah — a specific future individual from David’s line — who will physically rebuild the Temple and redeem the Jewish people. Reform Jews tend to reinterpret this as the ‘messianic age’: a future era of universal justice brought about through human effort and moral progress, without necessarily involving a specific individual. Jeremiah 23:5–8 is the named source for messianic hope.

Both Orthodox and Reform Judaism place responsibility on the Jewish people to actively work toward the conditions of the messianic age. Tikkun olam (‘repair of the world’) is the Jewish ethical concept that every act of justice, charity, compassion and righteousness contributes to repairing the broken world and hastening the time of redemption. This means the messianic hope is not passive waiting but active ethical engagement. A 12-mark Discuss answer on this topic should develop this active dimension alongside any divergence between Orthodox and Reform positions.
exam_tip_html: For the 5-mark ‘Explain two with sources’ question, use 2 Chronicles 7:1–3 (for the Shekhinah) or Jeremiah 23:5–8 (for the Messiah) as your named sources. Note the exact chapter and verse — examiners award the 5th mark only for a clearly identifiable, named source. For the 12-mark Discuss question on the Messiah, the Orthodox/Reform divergence is essential: develop both positions with equal depth. The most common student error is treating the Messiah as divine in Judaism — the Jewish Messiah is a human king, not a divine saviour in the Christian sense. SPaG rewards correct spelling of ‘Shekhinah’, ‘messianic’ and ‘monotheism’.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Almighty has four Edexcel-named characteristics: One (absolute monotheism), Creator (Genesis 2), Law-Giver and Judge. These shape how Jews understand their relationship with God in daily life.
  • The Shekhinah is the divine presence dwelling among the Jewish people, dramatically described in 2 Chronicles 7:1–3. Orthodox Jews associate it with the Temple; Reform Jews see it as present wherever Jews pray and act ethically.
  • The Messiah (from David’s line, Jeremiah 23:5–8) will inaugurate the messianic age of universal peace. Orthodox Jews expect a specific future individual; Reform Jews emphasise the messianic age brought by human ethical effort.

practice_questions.text: Outline three characteristics of the Almighty in Judaism.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for three characteristics with a brief explanation. Acceptable: One (absolute monotheism — the Almighty is the singular source of all existence, as stated in the Shema); Creator (brought all existence into being from nothing, forming humanity intimately as in Genesis 2); Law-Giver (source of all moral and religious law, including the Torah); Judge (holds all humanity accountable for their actions, motivating ethical living).

practice_questions.text: Describe the Jewish teaching about the Shekhinah.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks. Shekhinah means 'divine dwelling' or 'divine presence' (1 mark). 2 Chronicles 7:1-3 describes it descending as a cloud filling Solomon's Temple at its dedication (1 mark). It expresses how the transcendent Almighty can be encountered in human experience — in the Temple, synagogue, home and prayer (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Explain two Jewish beliefs about the Messiah.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per belief. Belief 1: the Messiah will be a human king from the line of King David who will restore Jewish sovereignty and rebuild the Temple — he is not divine but a specially anointed human leader; this belief reflects continued trust in the Almighty's promises. Belief 2: divergent understandings of the Messiah — Orthodox Jews expect a specific future individual who will physically rebuild the Temple; Reform Jews reinterpret this as the 'messianic age' of universal justice brought by human moral effort.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which belief in the Almighty as Creator shapes Jewish life today.
In your answer, include a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 + 2 marks + 1 for named source. Way 1: belief in the Almighty as Creator motivates environmental responsibility — creation is a gift from the Creator and Jews have a duty to protect it; this connects to Shabbat observance (rest for creation, not just humans). Way 2: belief that humanity is formed by the Almighty in an intimate act (Genesis 2 — the Almighty breathed life into Adam) gives every human being inherent dignity and worth, motivating justice and care for others. 5th mark: ‘Genesis 2 describes the Almighty forming man from dust and breathing life into him, showing the intimate relationship between Creator and creation.’

practice_questions.text:
'Belief in the Messiah is the most important belief in Judaism.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; justified conclusion. Arguments in support: Messianic hope gives Jews a future-oriented purpose and ethical motivation (tikkun olam); Jeremiah 23:5-8 anchors this in authoritative scripture; the hope for justice and universal peace is central to Jewish prayer (the Amidah includes prayers for the Messiah's coming); without this hope Judaism would lack its eschatological horizon. Arguments against: the Shema's declaration of monotheism (Deuteronomy 6:4 — 'Hear O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one') is the most foundational affirmation in Judaism — recited twice daily, at deathbeds; keeping the Mitzvot (commandments) is the most practical and immediate expression of Jewish faith; the covenant relationship with the Almighty (Genesis 17, Exodus 20) is prior to any messianic belief. Secure (7-9): Both sides; at least Jeremiah 23:5-8 named. Developing (4-6): One-sided. Emerging (1-3): Brief.

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between Orthodox and Reform Jewish beliefs about the Messiah.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per difference. Difference 1: Orthodox Jews believe in a personal Messiah — a specific future individual from David's line who will physically rebuild the Temple; Reform Jews tend to understand the messianic hope as a collective future era (the messianic age) rather than one specific person. Difference 2: Orthodox Jews see the coming of the Messiah as a miraculous divine act; many Reform Jews emphasise human moral effort (tikkun olam) as bringing about the conditions of justice and peace associated with the messianic age.

flashcard_questions.a: One (absolute monotheism), Creator, Law-Giver and Judge.
The divine presence of the Almighty; God's dwelling among the Jewish people.

flashcard_questions.a: A future human king from David's line who will restore justice and inaugurate universal peace.

flashcard_questions.q: Which prophet promises a righteous Branch from David's line?

flashcard_questions.a: An era of universal peace, justice and knowledge of God following the Messiah's coming.

flashcard_questions.a: Orthodox: specific future individual who rebuilds the Temple. Reform: collective messianic age through human moral effort.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Genesis 2 teach about the Almighty as Creator?
flashcard_questions.a: The Almighty formed humanity from dust and breathed life into them, showing intimate creative care.

glossary_terms.definition: The Jewish affirmation of God's absolute unity and oneness; central to Jewish theology.
The divine presence of the Almighty; in Jewish theology, God's presence that dwells among the Jewish people.
The anointed one; a future human king from the line of David who will restore justice and inaugurate the messianic age.
The era of universal peace, justice and knowledge of God that will follow the coming of the Messiah.
The branch of Judaism that adheres strictly to traditional Jewish law (halakha) as divinely revealed at Sinai.
The branch of Judaism that adapts Jewish practice to modern contexts, regarding the Torah as divinely inspired but open to reinterpretation.
